analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes federal college aid, raises the Pell Grant ceiling, and bans lender gifts and conflicts of interest.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 354-58, passed the Senate 83-8, and was signed into law on August 14, 2008 as Public Law 110-315.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill renews the main federal law governing college financial aid for five years. It raises the scheduled maximum Pell Grant for low-income students, adds consumer protections for people borrowing for college, and bans the gifts and revenue-sharing deals that had let student lenders pay colleges for preferred access to borrowers. It also requires colleges to publish the real net price of attendance and requires textbook publishers to disclose prices and sell books unbundled.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income students and their families gain from higher scheduled Pell Grants, year-round Pell eligibility, a shorter and simpler aid application, and net price calculators. Student borrowers gain disclosure rules, limits on prepayment penalties on private loans, and expanded loan forgiveness for public-service work like teaching, nursing, and firefighting. Members of the military and veterans gain in-state tuition protections and simplified interest rules.

how_it_helps.text: Schedules the maximum Pell Grant to rise from $6,000 in 2009-10 to $8,000 by 2014-15, and allows a second Pell Grant within one year for students attending school year-round.
Bans colleges' financial aid officers from taking gifts from lenders and bars colleges and lenders from revenue-sharing agreements and from trading preferred-lender status for perks.
Requires textbook publishers to disclose prices to faculty and to sell textbook bundles as separately priced items, and requires colleges to list textbook prices in course schedules.
Requires colleges to post net price calculators and puts lists of the highest-tuition and fastest-rising-cost schools on the Department of Education's College Navigator website.
Directs the Secretary of Education to simplify the federal student aid application, with the goal of cutting its data elements by half, and to offer a short EZ form for the poorest applicants.
Expands Perkins loan cancellation and loan repayment programs for public-service workers including teachers, nurses, firefighters, child care workers, prosecutors, and public defenders.
Reauthorizes TRIO, GEAR UP, work-study, and institutional aid for colleges serving low-income and minority students, and makes homeless and foster youth eligible for TRIO services.
Requires private student lenders to disclose loan terms clearly, gives borrowers 30 days to accept a loan offer and three days to cancel without penalty, and bars prepayment penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of higher scheduled Pell Grant authorizations and of extended federal insurance and interest subsidies for private lenders in the FFEL loan program through 2014 (2018 for loans to existing borrowers). Textbook publishers bear compliance costs and lost bundling revenue. Colleges bear new reporting and transparency requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill extends federal insurance and interest subsidies on FFEL loans through fiscal 2014, keeping public money flowing to private student lenders rather than moving lending to the cheaper direct federal loan program.
The higher Pell Grant ceiling is an authorization, not an appropriation; actual grant levels depend on later spending votes, so the scheduled increases are not guaranteed.
The bill admits foreign nursing schools and tightens but does not close participation by foreign medical schools in federal loan programs, subject to pass-rate and default-reimbursement conditions.
Most college-cost provisions are transparency requirements — published lists, reports, and calculators — rather than caps, so schools can keep raising prices as long as they explain themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to students are concrete: bigger scheduled Pell Grants, simpler aid applications, cleaner lender relationships, and better price information. The main weakness is that the cost-control and student-protection tools are mostly disclosure rules rather than hard limits, and the bill re-upes the expensive FFEL guarantee system for private lenders alongside the direct federal loan program. The 2008 credit crisis soon made that compromise moot — direct lending expanded rapidly within a year.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House 354-58, passed the Senate 83-8 after a short conference, and President Bush signed it into law as Public Law 110-315 on August 14, 2008.

narrative.text: The House Education and Labor Committee reported the bill amended by a 45-0 vote in December 2007.
The House passed it 354-58 on February 7, 2008, with every voting Democrat in favor and 135 Republicans joining them.
The Senate passed it with an amendment by unanimous consent on July 29, 2008; a conference committee reconciled the House and Senate versions within days.
The House adopted the conference report 380-49 on July 31, 2008, and the Senate agreed 83-8 the same day, with all 49 voting Democrats in favor.
President George W. Bush signed it on August 14, 2008 as Public Law 110-315.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Students and borrowers, who gained higher scheduled Pell Grants and new protections from conflicted lending arrangements. Private FFEL lenders also came out ahead, since the law renews their federal subsidies through 2014.

industries.industry: FFEL student loan lenders and guaranty agencies
industries.note: The law extends federal insurance and interest subsidies for bank-based student loans through 2014, locking in the lenders' role, while banning the gifts, revenue sharing, and advisory-council payments that had tied lenders to colleges. Borrowers get disclosure protections, but taxpayers keep subsidizing a parallel private-lender system alongside direct federal loans.

Private lenders must follow Truth in Lending disclosure rules, may not penalize prepayment, cannot imply college endorsement, and must tell borrowers about cheaper federal aid before the loan is signed.

Publishers must disclose prices to faculty, reveal prior edition dates and revision content, and sell bundles as separately priced items — a direct challenge to the practice of selling new editions with shrink-wrapped supplements.

The 90/10 rule is enforced with suspension of federal aid eligibility for repeat violators and public naming, but the law also expands for-profit eligibility by counting dual-enrollment high schoolers and liberal-arts degree schools as qualifying institutions.

Institutions gain reauthorized student aid, institutional aid, and grant programs, while accepting new transparency duties — net price calculators, cost-increase reports, and lender conflict-of-interest codes of conduct.
